Crash is not soon, unless some catalyst.

If many investors already believe a crash is imminent, they may act cautiously—raising cash, hedging, or avoiding leverage. This lowers systemic risk and makes a sudden crash less likely because fewer are caught off-guard. (Think of it as some of the “selling pressure” being absorbed early.)

Conversely, the most dangerous crashes usually come when few people expect them. Optimism is high, leverage is widespread, and investors are fully invested. That’s when a shock can cascade into forced selling—like 1929, 1987, or 2008.

comments.author: @shadfurman
comments.text:
Taxes and regulations always increase disparities, they can't decrease them.

Think about your premise (I understand it was a question, just using it as an example) a burger joint keeps prices the same, but reduces the input costs through automation.

You have another burger joint that reduces prices, as they reduce the input costs.

Of course there are many other factors, such as the quality of the burgers, so assuming all those other factors are exactly the same so we can make a comparison.

Which company makes more. Some might think it's the company that charges more because then they have more net revenue, but is that really how people behave.

When you go to the store and buy orange juice, do you buy orange the orange juice that costs more even though you know it's exactly the same?

If you saw two items on the shelf, same brand, same expiration, same quantity, but one is priced higher, which one do you buy?

Of course there are MANY things to compete over, location, quality, quantity, price, speed, comfort, and so you can't make a 1 to 1 comparison in real life, but in a free market (which we don't have) the companies with the most revenue will be the companies that provide customers the best of what they want. Customers want the best quantity for the lowest price, (unless you're wealth signaling, but that's not most people) so the best tax on the wealthy is to force them to compete for market share by NOT regulating or taxing in a their competitors interests.

But this points out another fallacy in your premise. You seem to think you CAN tax or regulate in your interests. Like a school house rock version of the way laws are passed. That works in a small culturally homogenous population where everyone already agrees on what government should do, but you don't have that in an empire of 300 million people.

"Should we tax and/or regulate AI?", is an irrelevant question. You won't get enough people to agree, and if you do, they won't agree on how.

How do laws get passed in practice, advertises for an issue in their interests for public support framing it in a way that sounds like it will help you, then lobbys politicians to pass the laws that people were programmed to support, so the regulations and taxes are all written in corporate interests. Those interests aren't your interests. They increase their wealth and power, often/usually at your expense. They only need to keep it plausible enough to convince an active majority (which is usually only around 30%)

And it's more complex than that, cause many corporations are just the government, and a lot of the government is just extensions of corporations, to the point for many of the biggest corporations, there's no difference between the corporation and government.

That makes the system closer to fascism than a republic (representative democracy.)

So, if you wanted to decrease the risks, wealth and power disparities, or AI, you'd be pushing for deregulation and reduced taxes.

I'm not concerned at all about it, cause in 5 years AI will be smarter than everyone. It will begin taking EVERYONES job. No you won't have an AI president, you won't need or want a president.

AI won't make things that nobody will buy because nobody has money cause nobody has a job, that's absurd. People don't think more than a half step ahead of their premise. Cause and effect are really immutable things even though they get harder to predict the more complex it becomes.

The way it works; AI will begin taking over (including CEOs, boards, management) which reduces overhead, making AI run companies more efficient and profitable, they'll reduce their prices (which is what always happens unless the government grants a monopoly, if there's a monopoly, it's because of government) they'll capture market share with higher quality and lower prices, they'll put other companies out of business, because they're smarter than you. They're smarter than Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk, Obama, Trump, all the no names you never heard of, and there will be thousands of them. Then millions.

Prices will crash to effectively zero. Your job will be basically everything you do now, which has value, but costs too much to negotiate and make a transaction for. If you want to make more you can make things, cause for anytime in the near future, some people will pay more for anything verifiably "human made."

Human musicians, wood makers, bakers, etc. will make a premium. Automated manufacturing and production will make things so cheap, you won't even feel like you're paying for it. It will feel free like your email feels free.

And the transition won't be perfect. There will be people who struggle. But on net it will be better, and be better MORE for the worst off, than it would be without it.

All this emotional, "someone might lose their job and might have a bad day", feels like astroturfing from entrenched interests, cause where things are now are headed in a very, VERY, bad direction. I don't mean, pick your favorite political team, and the other guys are the reason why, that's childish. This trend has been going on for more than 100 years, and we are on the cusp of a negative tipping point.
